name: dSFMT (MersenneTwister-Lab)
baseline: MT19937 (NumPy's reference-derived mt19937 implementation, as exposed by randomgen)
workload: randomgen's Generator.random(size=25000) producing uniform doubles in [0,1) from the DSFMT and MT19937 bit generators, minimum of 10 repeats of 100 calls, reported as ns per value, driven through Python/NumPy wrappers around the C code.
claimed_speedup: Uniform doubles: DSFMT 2.5 ns per value against MT19937 4.0 ns per value, about 1.6x faster (ratio derived from page data). Not faster on the other rows of the same table: Uint32 2.8 vs 2.5 ns, Uint64 4.2 vs 4.2 ns, Expon 6.3 vs 6.1 ns, Normal 10.1 vs 10.5 ns, Gamma 25.1 vs 20.8 ns. The SFMT row also shows Uniform 2.5 ns, so no gain over SFMT on this table.
hardware: Intel Cascade Lake (Family 6, Model 85, Stepping 7) at 3.1 GHz, Linux
tradeoffs: Generates IEEE 754 doubles in [1,2) and subtracts 1, so output is 52-bit mantissa only and the integer API is secondary (dsfmt_genrand_uint32 exists but there is no fill_array for integers). Period is a Mersenne exponent chosen at compile time (DSFMT_MEXP from 521 to 216091), and MEXP must match between dSFMT.c and the caller. Needs SSE2 or AltiVec for the SIMD path (the Makefile sets the flags) and an IEEE 754 platform. Not cryptographically secure, and the randomgen documentation recommends against any Mersenne Twister variant for new code.
caveats: Third-party numbers come from randomgen's Cython wrapper through NumPy's Generator, so the win is for bulk uniform doubles only and includes Python call overhead; compiler, compiler version and flags are not stated, which caps the tier at B. The MT19937 baseline is NumPy's implementation, not std::mt19937 or a fresh build of mt19937ar. The authors' own speed table and paper (Saito and Matsumoto, MCQMC 2008, claims dSFMT is fastest against MT, SFMT and WELL on 10^8 doubles) sit on math.sci.hiroshima-u.ac.jp, which was unreachable (host did not resolve and curl got 403), so that claim is known only from a search snippet and is not recorded as evidence. The dSFMT repo README, CHANGE-LOG and html/index.html contain no timing numbers; test.c only times dSFMT against itself (clock() around fill_array calls). The 313.5% vs 72.5% 'speed-up relative to NumPy' rows in the archived randomstate README give a similar picture but no hardware.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/MersenneTwister-Lab/dSFMT, then web search for dSFMT vs MT19937 throughput, which led to the randomgen performance page

name: giotto-ph (giotto-ai)
baseline: Ripser v1.2 (Ripser/ripser by Ulrich Bauer); also compared with GPU Ripser++ according to the release notes
workload: Wall-clock computation of Vietoris-Rips persistence barcodes on the Ripser benchmark datasets (sphere3, dragon, o3_1024, random16, fractal, o3_4096, torus4) as a function of thread count, from the README speedup figure.
claimed_speedup: README figure (speed-up against number of threads, read off the plotted SVG coordinates, so approximate and derived from page data): at 48 threads fractal about 23.7x, o3_4096 about 14.2x, random16 about 12.9x, o3_1024 about 10.2x, torus4 about 10.1x, sphere3 about 1.7x, dragon about 1.06x (peak about 1.5x at 5 threads). Release notes v0.1.0: 'establishes a new state of the art, surpassing even GPU-accelerated implementations such as Ripser++' on 'as few as 5-10 CPU cores'.
stars_or_usage: 59 stars; designed for integration with giotto-tda and pyflagser (README)
tradeoffs: AGPLv3 network copyleft (the README offers a separate licence on request via the L2F team); Python API with a C++ backend, installed as wheels. Only Vietoris-Rips filtrations. The optional edge collapse (reimplementation of GUDHI's algorithm) does not help every dataset, and speedup depends on dataset size and homology dimension: shallow computations such as dragon up to dimension 1 barely scale.
caveats: The README states the scaling claim only as a figure and points to the arXiv paper 2107.05412, which could not be opened (arXiv host does not resolve here). From search snippets the paper says giotto-ph is always faster than Ripser v1.2 above one thread, performs about like Ripser v1.2 on a single thread, and skips GUDHI and Eirene comparisons because Ripser is faster than both; those statements are snippet-only. The figure's y axis is labelled speed-up and its reference run is not named on the SVG, so the plotted values are most likely scaling against giotto-ph's own single-thread run, not a head-to-head with Ripser. No CPU model, core count (axis reaches 48 threads), compiler or flags appear in the README, release notes or repo, and the repo has no benchmark folder or benchmark code. Ripser++ numbers (GPU baseline) were not found in any reachable page. Ripserer.jl issue #168 (the lead) only mentions giotto-tda as a package that supports the feature the poster asked about, and a maintainer reply that results were mixed; it has no speed data.

name: kiwi (nucleic, C++ Cassowary solver)
baseline: original Cassowary C++ solver (cassowary-0.60 assumed; the README does not give a version)
workload: Constraint solving with the Cassowary algorithm for typical user-interface layout use cases; the README does not describe the workload.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Kiwi ranges from 10x to 500x faster than the original Cassowary solver with typical use cases gaining a 40x improvement. Memory savings are consistently > 5x.'
tradeoffs: Not a refactoring of the original, so behaviour differs: stay constraints were dropped (emulate with edit variables or equality constraints), and strengths are plain floating point numbers instead of lexicographic ordering, so in rare corner cases many weak constraints can outweigh a medium one. Header-only C++ with hand-rolled Python bindings. Internally uses Loki's AssocVector, which the docs say gives a 2x speedup over std::map.
caveats: Numbers only in README prose and mirrored in docs/source/index.rst and downstream package descriptions: no workload, hardware, compiler, flags, Cassowary version or benchmark code against Cassowary is published. The repo's benchmarks directory (enaml_like_benchmark.cpp built with g++ -O2, and a Python variant using perf) measures only kiwi itself, mainly to compare internal map types. The date of the 10x-500x range and the 40x 'typical' figure is not stated (the licence copyright line starts at 2013), and they cannot be reproduced from the repo. The 2x over std::map statement is likewise a docs claim with no table. amoeba (starwing, C) says it improves on kiwi's suggest path but gives no numbers.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/nucleic/kiwi README, benchmarks directory and docs/source/basis/solver_internals.rst

name: hilbert_curves (rawrunprotected)
baseline: classic iterative xy2d Hilbert index loop with per-level quadrant rotation (Wikipedia-style loop; measured as loop_rotation in the Rust port benchmark), not literally the Hacker's Delight code
workload: Evidence is for a Rust port, not this repo: the magic_bits encoder in Filyus/packed_spatial_index (a port of this repo's hilbertXYToIndex) against its loop_rotation encoder, encoding 100,000 random (u16, u16) points into an output buffer with Criterion, single pinned core.
claimed_speedup: Port benchmark: magic_bits 185 us per 100k points (541 Melem/s) against loop_rotation 998 us (100 Melem/s), about 5.4x (derived from page data); also 3.5x faster than the fast_hilbert crate (644 us, 155 Melem/s) and within a few percent of static_aabb2d_index's reference encoder (183 us). The repo itself only says 'the world's fastest implementations of 2D and 3D hilbert curve functions' with no numbers.
compiler_and_flags: Rust, Cargo bench profile with lto = true and codegen-units = 1 (from Cargo.toml); rustc version and RUSTFLAGS for this table not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 (Zen 5 laptop), benchmark thread pinned to one performance core
license: public domain (README statement, no LICENSE file)
stars_or_usage: 82 stars; ported by Filyus/packed_spatial_index (Rust) and jbenison/hilbert (64-bit C++)
tradeoffs: Branchless XOR/AND/shift arithmetic, constant time in curve order, 16 bits per axis in 2D (32-bit index) and a table-driven 3D conversion between Morton and Hilbert order that takes 3 index bits per level (a 32-bit code covers about 10 levels). Fastest when iterations are independent; the Rust port's own notes say a table-driven LUT wins in single-call dependent-accumulation latency loops.
caveats: The repo has four commits, a README with no numbers, and a single hilbert_curves.cpp; the author's explanation posts (threadlocalmutex.com) were unreachable. The only numbers found are for a Rust port in another repo, so they support the algorithm, not this exact C++ file, and the hardware and Rust settings are not the C++ ones. The README dedication to the public domain is informal (no LICENSE file, no CC0 text) and carries no patent grant. The baseline loop is the port author's own Rust loop_rotation, not Hacker's Delight code, and libmorton was not part of any comparison found. Other Hilbert libraries found (becheran/fast-hilbert LUT, Wunkolo/qHilbert SIMD) benchmark against different baselines and do not measure this code; jbenison/hilbert (64-bit port) lists about 2 ns per call with no baseline. Treat as tier C by indirect evidence; if the verifier will not accept port evidence, the repo alone is tier D.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/rawrunprotected/hilbert_curves README, then the Filyus/packed_spatial_index hilbert2d.rs source header and docs/performance.md

name: libmorton (Forceflow)
baseline: libmorton's own lookup-table methods (LUT and LUT Shifted) for 3D Morton encode and decode; the listed loop-based and magic-bits baselines have numbers only in the author's blog posts, which were unreachable
workload: 3D Morton encode and decode of 512^3 = 134,217,728 codes, 32-bit and 64-bit, with linearly increasing and random inputs, averaged over 5 runs, using libmorton's own test harness (kevinhartman/libmorton fork) as reported in the morton-nd README.
claimed_speedup: 32-bit 3D encode: BMI2 530.421 ms (linear) and 536.726 ms (random) against LUT 668.371 and 665.673 ms, about 1.26x and 1.24x. 32-bit 3D decode: BMI2 560.478 and 3159.143 ms against LUT 1033.880 and 3605.081 ms, about 1.84x and 1.14x. 64-bit 3D encode: BMI2 524.044 and 563.434 ms against LUT 909.336 and 929.829 ms, about 1.74x and 1.65x (all ratios derived from page data). README prose: BMI2 'is definitely a faster method when compared to the standard case'.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.1.0 on macOS 11.1 with -O3 -DNDEBUG; the flag that enables the BMI2 path (for example -mbmi2 or -march) is not stated
stars_or_usage: 667 stars; cited as used by Esri, Cesium Ion and CLAIRE
tradeoffs: Header-only C++11 with 2D and 3D, 16/32/64-bit coordinates. The fast path needs BMI2 (Intel Haswell or newer, AMD Zen or newer) enabled at compile time; AVX512 BITALG support is experimental. Lookup-table methods use memory and cache that the magic-bits and BMI2 paths avoid.
caveats: The repo README contains no numbers; it points to three forceflow.be blog posts (2013 bit-interleaving, 2016 libmorton, 2016 BMI2) that hold the real benchmarks, and that host did not resolve here. The only numbers found are third-party and compare libmorton's BMI2 path with libmorton's own LUT paths, so no recognizable external incumbent and none of the listed loop or magic-bits baselines is measured; by the catalog rules this is a weak qualification and the tier is capped at C. PR #40 (AVX512 vs BMI2 on an i7-1065G7, 'proper release-mode build', compiler not stated) shows the experimental AVX512 path roughly equal to BMI2, slightly slower in some rows (64-bit 1.060 ms vs 0.915 ms) and slightly faster in others (0.894 ms vs 1.082 ms). The morton-nd authors report their generated code is as fast as libmorton's hand-written code, so these numbers are a morton-nd versus libmorton parity check as well.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/Forceflow/libmorton README, then web search for libmorton benchmarks, which led to the morton-nd README and libmorton PR #40
